questions.stem: Which of these is an education strategy for sustainable resource management?
options: A school program teaching students how to cut household energy use
A rebate that pays part of the cost of installing rooftop solar panels
A fine charged to a company that discharges waste into a river
A new turbine design that generates more power from low winds
questions.explanation: Education strategies change behaviour by increasing knowledge and awareness. Rebates and fines are economic strategies, and a better turbine is a science and technology strategy.

questions.stem: Which of these is a science and technology strategy?
options: Offering grants to farmers who fence cattle out of creeks and rivers
Developing recirculating tanks that treat and reuse fish farm water
Running television advertisements that encourage people to save water
Charging households for each kilolitre of water they draw from the mains
questions.explanation: Recirculating aquaculture systems are a technological solution that reduces water use and waste discharge. Advertisements are education, and per-kilolitre charges and grants are economic strategies.

questions.stem: Economic strategies for sustainable resource management work mainly by:
options: using police powers to arrest people who damage the environment
using financial incentives and disincentives to change behaviour
using research to invent new ways of producing goods and services
using information campaigns to raise people's awareness of issues
questions.explanation: Economic strategies change the costs and rewards of actions, through grants, rebates, taxes, fines and pricing. Research is science and technology, and campaigns are education.

questions.stem: Why is an education strategy often combined with economic or technological strategies rather than used alone?
options: Education strategies are illegal unless a government has first passed a new law
People who receive education always choose the least sustainable option
Education strategies work only for industries, never for households
Awareness may not change behaviour if the sustainable choice costs more
questions.explanation: People may understand an issue but still not act if the sustainable option is expensive or inconvenient. Combining education with incentives or better technology makes the sustainable choice easier and cheaper.

questions.stem: A council wants to reduce household food waste going to landfill. Which combination uses all three types of strategy?
options: Composting workshops, a leaflet about food waste, and a website explaining how to plan meals
A fine for overfull bins, a tax on landfill, and a higher fee for collecting large rubbish bins
A new food-organics bin, a new composting facility, and new trucks to collect organic waste
Composting workshops, a new food-organics bin collection, and a lower fee for smaller rubbish bins
questions.explanation: Workshops are education, a food-organics collection is science and technology, and lower fees for smaller bins are an economic incentive. The other combinations use only one type of strategy each.

questions.stem: Traditional economics measures economic growth mainly by:
options: gross domestic product (GDP)
the size of the ecological footprint
the number of protected species
the area of land in national parks
questions.explanation: Traditional economics focuses on GDP, the total value of goods and services produced. Green economics argues that GDP leaves out environmental costs and the loss of natural resources.

questions.stem: Why do green economists argue that GDP can give a misleading picture of a country's wellbeing?
options: GDP counts only the value of goods that are exported, so it ignores most local spending
GDP falls whenever forests are logged, so it always undervalues the forestry industry
GDP includes the value of all ecosystem services, so it double counts nature's benefits
GDP rises with clean-up spending but ignores the loss of natural resources
questions.explanation: Spending to repair environmental damage adds to GDP, while depleting forests, fisheries or soils is not subtracted. GDP rises, not falls, when timber is harvested and sold.

questions.stem: Green economics differs from traditional economics mainly because it:
options: requires every resource to be owned and managed by the government, not businesses
uses incentives and disincentives so prices reflect environmental costs
rejects all trade and money, and relies only on bartering between local communities
aims to increase GDP as quickly as possible regardless of environmental damage
questions.explanation: Green economics builds environmental values into decision making, using taxes, charges, grants and rebates to reward sustainable choices and penalise harmful ones. It still uses markets and money.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an economic incentive?
options: A tax charged for each tonne of waste sent to landfill
A fine for illegally clearing native vegetation
A fee charged for each visit to a national park
A rebate on the cost of an energy-efficient heat pump
questions.explanation: An incentive rewards a sustainable choice, as a rebate does by lowering its cost. Taxes, fines and fees are disincentives or pricing tools that make harmful or heavy use more expensive.

questions.stem: A government offers grants to farmers to plant native shelter belts along creeks. How does this strategy work?
options: It requires farmers to sell their land to the government for revegetation
It lowers the cost of a sustainable practice, so more farmers adopt it
It punishes farmers who have cleared creeks, so they stop clearing land
It charges farmers for each megalitre of water taken from the creeks
questions.explanation: A grant is an incentive: it pays part of the cost of an action with environmental benefits, encouraging adoption. Charging for water is user pays, and punishing clearing is a disincentive.

questions.stem: A state offers interest-free loans for households to install insulation and efficient heating. Which outcome best indicates the strategy is working as intended?
options: Electricity prices rise for all households because fewer homes buy power
Household electricity use per home falls in homes that took up the loans
The number of loan applications falls each year after the scheme begins
Households with loans use more electricity because heating is now cheaper
questions.explanation: The aim is to cut energy use and emissions, so lower electricity use in participating homes is the evidence of success. Using more energy because heating is cheaper would undermine the strategy.

questions.stem: The polluter pays principle means that:
options: governments use taxpayers' money to clean up pollution caused by industries
communities affected by pollution pay to have it removed from their area
consumers pay a deposit when they buy a product, refunded when it is returned
those who cause pollution bear the cost of preventing or repairing the damage
questions.explanation: Under polluter pays, the party responsible for pollution pays, through fines, taxes or clean-up costs. Taxpayer-funded clean-up shifts the cost away from the polluter, which is what the principle aims to avoid.

questions.stem: A factory is fined after a spill of chemicals into an estuary and ordered to pay for the clean-up. Which principle is being applied?
options: Precautionary principle
Polluter pays
User pays
Intergenerational equity
questions.explanation: The factory caused the pollution and is paying for it, which is polluter pays. User pays charges people for using a resource, such as water or park entry.

questions.stem: A tax is charged on each tonne of carbon dioxide a power station emits. How is this expected to reduce emissions?
options: It bans all emissions immediately, so power stations must close down
It rewards firms that emit more, so they compete to produce more CO2
It lowers the price of fossil fuels, so less coal needs to be burnt
It makes emitting more expensive, so firms invest in cleaner energy
questions.explanation: A carbon tax is a disincentive: by adding a cost to each tonne emitted, it makes low-emission options relatively cheaper. It does not ban emissions outright.

questions.stem: A government has a choice: fine farms that let fertiliser run into a river, or pay farms to install buffer strips. Which statement best compares the two strategies?
options: Fines and grants have identical effects, so there is no reason to prefer either one
Grants are disincentives and fines are incentives, so both make pollution cheaper
Fines apply polluter pays but need monitoring; grants encourage action but use public money
Fines use public money and grants make farmers pay, so both breach polluter pays
questions.explanation: A fine is a disincentive that makes the polluter pay, but diffuse runoff is hard to trace to one farm. A grant is an incentive that can quickly change practice, but the public rather than the polluter bears the cost.

questions.stem: A negative externality is:
options: a cost of an activity borne by others and not included in its price
a benefit of an activity received by people who did not pay for it
a tax that a government adds to the price of imported goods
a cost that the producer pays directly for raw materials and labour
questions.explanation: A negative externality, such as pollution harming people downstream, is a cost imposed on third parties and not paid by the producer or buyer. Real cost pricing aims to include it in the price.

questions.stem: Real cost pricing would make electricity generated from coal more expensive because it:
options: removes the cost of mining coal from the price of the electricity
adds the cost of building new wind farms to coal-fired electricity
lowers the price of renewable energy by banning coal-fired power
adds the costs of air pollution and climate change to the price
questions.explanation: Real cost pricing includes negative externalities, such as health damage from air pollution and the costs of climate change, in the price of a product. This lets cleaner options compete fairly.

questions.stem: Two brands of farmed fish sell at the same price. One farm treats its waste and monitors the seabed; the other discharges waste untreated. Which statement best applies the real cost pricing principle?
options: The first farm's fish should be cheaper, because waste treatment lowers its costs to nothing
Externalities apply only to energy, so real cost pricing cannot be used for aquaculture
The untreated waste is an externality, so the second farm's true cost is higher than its price
Both brands have the same real cost, because they sell at exactly the same shop price
questions.explanation: The second farm passes the cost of its pollution on to the environment and other users, so its price hides part of the real cost. Real cost pricing would include that externality, making its fish dearer.

questions.stem: Which is an example of the user pays principle?
options: Fining a company for releasing smoke above its set limit
Giving a rebate for buying an energy-efficient fridge
Running a campaign about the dangers of littering
Charging households for each kilolitre of water they use
questions.explanation: User pays charges people according to how much of a resource or service they use, as volumetric water charges do. A fine for pollution applies polluter pays.

questions.stem: A state charges a fee to enter its national parks and uses the money for track maintenance. Which principle does this illustrate?
options: Polluter pays, because every visitor to a park is causing serious pollution
Intragenerational equity, because only the wealthiest people can enter parks
Real cost pricing, because the fee adds the cost of climate change to entry
User pays, because visitors contribute to the costs of the parks they use
questions.explanation: Park entry fees ask the people who use a resource to help pay for its management, which is user pays. Visiting a park is a use, not pollution.

questions.stem: A town's water price is changed from a flat annual charge to a charge for each kilolitre used. What change in water use is most likely?
options: Use stays the same, because water price never affects household behaviour
Use falls only in winter, because people cannot use water in the cold
Use falls, because each extra kilolitre now costs the household money
Use rises, because households now feel they have paid for unlimited water
questions.explanation: Under a flat charge the cost of using more water is zero, so there is little reason to save. Volumetric pricing gives a direct financial reason to cut use, applying user pays.

questions.stem: Most of Tasmania's electricity is generated from which source?
options: Nuclear power stations
Diesel generators
Hydro-electric dams
Coal-fired power stations
questions.explanation: Tasmania's electricity system is built largely on hydro-electric power, supplemented by wind. Tasmania has no coal-fired or nuclear power stations generating its grid electricity.

questions.stem: Tasmania has legislated a target to generate renewable electricity equal to 200% of its needs by 2040. Which aim does this target mainly serve?
options: Ending all electricity connections between Tasmania and the mainland
Producing surplus renewable energy to export and to power new industries
Replacing Tasmania's coal-fired power stations with new hydro-electric dams
Reducing Tasmania's electricity production so that less water is stored
questions.explanation: Having already met 100% renewable electricity, Tasmania set the target to roughly double renewable generation so surplus can be exported and used for new industries such as green hydrogen. Tasmania has no coal-fired power stations to replace.

questions.stem: Tasmania's net greenhouse gas emissions have been reported at or below zero. Which explanation do state reports give as the main reason?
options: Tasmanian farms stopped keeping cattle and sheep, so agriculture produces no methane
Tasmanian industry closed entirely, so the state produces no energy emissions at all
Forests became a carbon sink as native forest harvesting fell and regrowth rose
All Tasmanian vehicles were converted to electric power, ending transport emissions
questions.explanation: State reporting attributes net zero mainly to the land use, land use change and forestry sector: reduced native forest harvesting and regrowth made Tasmania's forests a net carbon sink, alongside renewable electricity. Transport and agriculture still produce substantial emissions.

questions.stem: Because Tasmania's electricity is mostly renewable, which local strategy would most reduce the state's remaining energy emissions?
options: Building more hydro-electric dams to replace the state's coal power stations
Encouraging households to switch from electric heat pumps to gas heaters
Importing more petrol so that fuel prices fall for Tasmanian drivers
Replacing petrol and diesel vehicles with electric ones using grid power
questions.explanation: With a largely renewable grid, emissions come mainly from burning fuels, especially in transport, so electrifying vehicles moves that energy use onto renewable electricity. Switching heat pumps to gas would add fossil fuel emissions.

questions.stem: Tasmania's forests have stored a large amount of carbon. Why do state reports warn that this sink is not guaranteed into the future?
options: Bushfires, drought, heatwaves and disease could release carbon and slow forest growth
Forests stop absorbing carbon once they are protected in reserves and national parks
Hydro-electric dams use up the carbon that forests store, emptying the sink over time
Carbon stored in trees turns into methane as they age, which is released each summer
questions.explanation: Climate change increases the risk of fire, drought and heat stress, which can release stored carbon and reduce forest growth. Protected forests continue to store carbon; reservation does not stop uptake.

questions.stem: Which strategy for energy in Tasmania is correctly matched to its strategy type?
options: A rebate for installing efficient heat pumps: education
A school energy-saving competition: economics
A public talk on electric vehicles: science and technology
Pumped hydro to back up wind power: science and technology
questions.explanation: Pumped hydro is an engineering solution that stores energy when wind is plentiful, so it is a science and technology strategy. A rebate is economic, and a competition or public talk is education.

questions.stem: Large hydro-electric schemes generate renewable electricity. Which environmental cost must they still manage?
options: Altered river flows and habitat flooded by the dams' storage lakes
High carbon dioxide emissions from burning water in the turbines
Release of acid rain from the cooling towers beside each dam
Radioactive waste produced by the turbines during generation
questions.explanation: Dams flood valleys and change the timing, temperature and volume of river flows, affecting aquatic ecosystems. Hydro-electricity does not burn anything, so it produces no combustion emissions or acid rain.

questions.stem: Which Tasmanian body regulates the environmental impacts of marine finfish farms through environmental licences?
options: The Environment Protection Authority (EPA)
The Australian Bureau of Meteorology
The Tasmanian Fire Service
The Reserve Bank of Australia
questions.explanation: The EPA issues environmental licences for finfish farms with conditions on monitoring and environmental performance. The other bodies have no role in regulating aquaculture.

questions.stem: Environmental licences for Tasmanian salmon farms include conditions requiring broadscale monitoring of the seabed and water. What is the main purpose of this monitoring?
options: To count the number of salmon in each pen so that the farms can set their prices
To measure rainfall at each farm so that farmers know when to harvest the fish
To prove that fish farms have no effect at all on the surrounding ecosystems
To detect impacts such as organic build-up early so that farming can be adjusted
questions.explanation: Ongoing monitoring of benthic condition and water quality shows whether a farm is exceeding acceptable impacts, so regulators can require changes such as lower stocking. Monitoring tests impacts; it does not assume there are none.

questions.stem: A salmon company leaves a lease empty for several months between production cycles. Why does this fallowing reduce environmental impact?
options: It lets wild fish eat the leftover feed so that the farm saves money
It lets salt build up in the sediment, which kills harmful bacteria
It lets the pens be moved inland where waste cannot reach the sea
It lets the seabed recover as accumulated organic waste breaks down
questions.explanation: Without new feed and faeces, bacteria can break down the organic matter under the pens and benthic communities can recover. Fallowing is a management practice informed by seabed monitoring.

questions.stem: Macquarie Harbour, a sheltered harbour on Tasmania's west coast, has had low dissolved oxygen in deep water and is home to the endangered Maugean skate. Why is intensive salmon farming a particular concern there?
options: Salmon farms add fresh water to the harbour, which removes all its dissolved oxygen
Salmon pens block sunlight from the deep water, where skates photosynthesise
Farmed salmon prey mainly on adult skates, which removes the breeding population
Organic waste from farms adds oxygen demand in water that already exchanges slowly
questions.explanation: The harbour's deep water is renewed slowly, and decomposition of farm waste increases biological oxygen demand, worsening low oxygen in skate habitat. Skates are animals and do not photosynthesise.

questions.stem: Which is a science and technology strategy for reducing the impact of salmon farming?
options: Teaching consumers how to read sustainable seafood labels
Charging companies a fee for each tonne of fish produced
Moving pens to deeper, more exposed sites where waste disperses
Fining companies that exceed the limits set in their licences
questions.explanation: Siting farms in deeper, more exposed water, with engineering to suit, is a technological response that helps waste disperse and limits local build-up. Fines and fees are economic, and labelling campaigns are education.

questions.stem: Some consumers choose salmon carrying a sustainability certification label. Which type of strategy does the label mainly rely on?
options: Economics, by fining farms that fail to meet the certification standards
Legislation, by making it illegal to sell any salmon that is not certified
Education, by informing buyers so they can pick more sustainable products
Science and technology, by redesigning salmon pens to hold less fish waste
questions.explanation: A label informs consumers, who can then reward better practice through what they buy, so it rests on education and awareness. Certification is voluntary, not a legal requirement.

questions.stem: A fish farm is required to pay a licence fee that funds independent environmental monitoring of the waterway it uses. Which principle is best illustrated?
options: Intergenerational equity, because the fee is paid by future generations
Real cost pricing, because the fee lowers the price of farmed fish in shops
Precautionary principle, because the fee is paid only after damage is proven
User or polluter pays, because the industry meets the cost of managing its impact
questions.explanation: The industry that uses the waterway and may pollute it pays for the monitoring, rather than taxpayers, which applies user pays and polluter pays. Real cost pricing would raise, not lower, the price of the product.

questions.stem: University marine scientists study how far waste spreads from fish pens using sediment cores and water sampling. How does this research support sustainable management?
options: It increases the number of fish that can be grown, whatever the impact
It gives evidence for setting stocking limits and siting farms
It replaces the need for any regulation of fish farms by the government
It proves that fish farms always improve water quality in every location
questions.explanation: Scientific data allow regulators and companies to set limits and site farms where impacts are acceptable. Research informs regulation rather than replacing it, and it tests impacts rather than assuming a result.

questions.stem: Which proposal best combines all three strategy types to make aquaculture in a Tasmanian estuary more sustainable?
options: Community information sessions, school excursions to farms, and a seafood website
Seabed monitoring, a levy on high-impact leases, and community info sessions
Seabed monitoring research, new underwater cameras, and better feed-pellet designs
A levy on high-impact leases, fines for spills, and a fee for each tonne of fish
questions.explanation: Monitoring research is science and technology, a levy is economic, and information sessions are education. The other options each rely on one strategy type only.
